title: The Blasted Heath
subtitle: A one-evening scenario adapted from H. P. Lovecraft’s “The Colour Out of Space” (1927)

meta.era: October 1925, the hills west of Arkham, Massachusetts

warnings: Body horror (people and animals greying and crumbling)
A family’s deaths, in the past
credits: Adapted for The Case File from H. P. Lovecraft’s story “The Colour Out of Space”, first published in 1927 and now in the public domain. Scenario text, handouts and investigators are original to this pack.

sections.title: At a glance
sections.text:
In October 1925 the Arkham Water Commission is about to flood a quiet valley west of town to make a new reservoir. The investigators are sent to finish the survey after the chief surveyor comes back to Arkham sick. At the heart of the valley lies five acres of grey, dead ground the farmers call the blasted heath, and in the middle of it, the old Gardner well.

Forty-three years ago something fell out of the sky beside that well. It destroyed the Gardner family, and most of it went back up into the sky. Not all of it. What stayed behind has been waiting in the well, and the survey’s young chainman has just drunk from it.

The investigators have one night to understand what is happening and decide what to do: seal the well, save the boy, or run.

### Investigators
Five ready-made investigators come with this pack: a civil engineer, a doctor, a geologist, a newspaper reporter and a survey rodman. Players pick them when they join. If players bring their own, each needs a reason to join a reservoir survey: hired hand, Miskatonic academic, journalist, county official or a friend of one of these.

### Shape of the evening
- Act 1, Arkham (30 minutes): the job, and optional research.
- Act 2, the valley (45 minutes): the survey camp, the heath and old Ammi Pierce.
- Act 3, the Gardner place (45 minutes): the ruined farm, the well, the missing chainman.
- Act 4, night on the heath (60 minutes): the colour wakes.

sections.title: What really happened
sections.text:
In June 1882 a meteorite fell beside Nahum Gardner’s well. Professors from Miskatonic University found it soft, hot and shrinking. It showed bands of a colour no spectroscope could place. Inside was a brittle globule of that colour, which burst when struck. The stone was hit by lightning in a storm and was gone by the next week.

It was not gone. Something from inside it had gone down into the well. Over the next year the Gardner farm turned strange: fruit grew huge and bitter, animals left wrong tracks in the snow, plants glowed faintly at night. Then the colour began to feed. The livestock greyed and crumbled. Nahum’s wife went mad. His sons went to the well and did not come back. Nahum himself crumbled to grey dust in his kitchen in 1883.

Ammi Pierce, the Gardners’ only friend, brought men from Arkham to the farm that autumn. That night they watched the colour pour up out of the well and shoot into the sky. Ammi alone saw a small piece of it fall back and sink into the well.

That fragment has been feeding slowly ever since. The dead ground grows a little every year. In 1925 the survey party camped beside the heath. The chief surveyor, Ezra Lund, and the young chainman, Silas Coombs, drank from the well: the water looked clear and tasted sweet. Lund fell ill and went home. Silas is staying, and the colour has him. Fed on him, it is nearly strong enough to rise. Tonight it will try.

sections.title: Running the colour
sections.text:
The colour is not a creature with a body. It is something alive in the way a fire is alive. It cannot be shot, stabbed, burned or reasoned with. Describe it only by what it does to things: grey ash where grass was, light that comes from leaves rather than falling on them, a colour at the edge of sight that no one can name and everyone remembers.

### What it does
- By day it stays in the well water. Anyone who drinks the water must make a Hard CON roll. On a failure they are touched: their skin slowly greys and they feel drawn to the well. Nothing worse happens unless they stay near the heath.
- At night its reach spreads about fifty yards from the well. Every ten minutes spent inside the reach costs 1 hit point, and lamp flames look dull and grey.
- When it pours out of the well (Act 4), anyone within ten yards must make a POW roll each round. On a failure they stand still, fascinated, and lose 1D3 hit points. Someone else can drag them clear with a STR roll.
- People and animals it drains to nothing crumble into grey dust.

### How it can be stopped
- Burying it. Earth and stone dull it, as the 1882 laboratory notes hint (Handout 4). Collapsing the well onto it with the survey’s blasting powder seals it in for good, or at least until the reservoir drowns it under eighty feet of water.
- Starving it. If Silas and the horses are kept off the heath, it cannot rise tonight. It will sink back and wait, and the investigators will need another plan.
- Letting it go. If it feeds enough it rises into the sky as it did in 1883, and may leave another piece behind.

The point is not a fight. Let the investigators work out that the well is the key, and give them a frightening, physical task to do there.

sections.title: Act 1: The commission
sections.text:
The investigators meet Harlan P. Weeks of the Arkham Water Commission at Arkham town hall on a cold Monday morning. Share Handout 1 (the letter of engagement) and Handout 2 (the survey map).

Weeks is a fussy, decent man in a hurry. The valley is to be flooded in the spring and the survey is two weeks behind. Ezra Lund, the chief surveyor, came back on Saturday with a fever. The camp is at Pierce’s Corner, with a chainman, Silas Coombs, keeping it. There is blasting powder in the camp stores: the old Gardner well must be filled before flooding, and Weeks would be grateful if they saw to it.

If asked about the heath, Weeks laughs it off: farmers’ talk, poor soil, an old family that died out. He has never been there.

### Optional research
- Arkham Advertiser offices (Library Use): the back issues for June 1882 hold the report of the falling stone. Share Handout 3.
- Miskatonic University library (Library Use, or the geologist simply asks a colleague): the 1882 laboratory notes on the specimen. Share Handout 4. This is the one that hints that stone and earth dull the colour.
- Ezra Lund at the Arkham hospital (Medicine or Persuade to be let in): Lund is grey at the fingertips, his hair coming out in brittle tufts. He talks fondly of the sweetest water he ever drank and asks, twice, whether the boy is still out there. A doctor can tell that the illness is nothing they have seen. Seeing Lund costs 0/1D3 Sanity.

sections.title: Act 2: The valley
sections.text:
The road west of Arkham climbs into old, steep, wooded hills. Farms thin out. The few locals the investigators pass are polite and say nothing useful, except that nobody from the valley has taken water from the Gardner place in forty years.

The survey camp at Pierce’s Corner is two canvas tents, a cook fire, a Ford truck and two horses on a picket line, about two hundred yards from the edge of the heath.

### Silas Coombs
Silas, nineteen and cheerful, is glad of company. He works hard, talks too much and keeps his hands in his pockets. A Spot Hidden or a handshake shows his fingertips are grey, like ash under the skin. He says it is chalk from the survey stakes. A Psychology roll shows he is lying to himself rather than to them. He goes back to the heath whenever he can, and offers the investigators water from the well in a tin cup. Seeing his hands properly costs 0/1D3 Sanity (preset 3).

### The blasted heath
Five acres of grey, powdery ground where nothing grows. Dead trees stand around it, bleached white. The ground crunches. Survey stakes from last week are already greyed where they touch the soil. Walking onto it by daylight costs 0/1 Sanity (preset 1).

A Natural World or Science (Geology) roll shows this is not burned ground, salt or poison. The soil has been emptied. The geologist can measure where the grey ends; comparing with Lund’s stakes shows it has crept outward since last week.

### Ammi Pierce
Ammi lives alone in a sagging farmhouse on the old road, a quarter mile from the heath. He is near eighty, sharp-eyed and frightened. He will not go near the heath and is relieved that the reservoir will drown it. With a Persuade or Charm roll, or a cup of something warm and an hour of patience, he tells the Gardners’ story as written under What really happened, in his own slow way.

The most important thing he says, and only if asked what became of it: “Most of it went up. Not all. I seen a bit of it fall back, and go down in that well, and I never told a soul.”

He keeps a yellowed copy of the 1882 Advertiser in his Bible. If the investigators didn’t find it in Arkham, share Handout 3 here.

sections.title: Act 3: The Gardner place
sections.text:
The Gardner farmhouse stands near the middle of the heath: grey boards, fallen roof, the barn collapsed. The well is in the yard, a ring of old stones with a rotted wooden cover. Silas has pulled the cover aside.

### The house
- The kitchen: a rocking chair and, in the dust around it, a shape like something long ago lying there. A Spot Hidden finds a buckled tin almanac box under the floorboards. Share Handout 5 (Nahum Gardner’s almanac). Reading the last pages costs 0/1D2 Sanity (preset 2).
- Upstairs: a door barred from the outside, a room with scratches inside the door. This is where Nahum kept his wife. Nothing is there now.

### The well
The water is clear and very still, about twenty feet down. Lowering a lantern shows the bottom is mud and old bones: cattle, a dog, and two human skulls. Seeing them costs 1/1D4 Sanity (preset 4). A Listen roll at the well hears a sound like breath going in and never coming out.

### Silas’s field book
Silas’s pocket notebook lies on the well stones, where he sat to drink this morning. Share Handout 6. The last entries make it plain he knows something is wrong and cannot stop himself going back.

### The blasting powder
In the camp stores: a box of blasting powder, a coil of fuse and caps, meant for filling the well and clearing stumps. The engineer knows how to use it. Setting a charge to collapse the well takes a Demolitions roll (or a Hard Mechanical Repair roll, or a Hard INT roll for someone shown how). Done by daylight it is safe and quick. Done at night, inside the reach, it is the climax.

sections.title: Act 4: Night on the heath
sections.text:
However the investigators spend the afternoon, the night comes. If they leave the valley, Silas stays, and they will need a good reason to come back.

### Timeline
- Dusk: insects fall silent. The heath stays faintly visible after the sun has gone, as if lit from underneath.
- Nine o’clock: the dead trees around the heath stir and sway in still air. Their tips glow. 0/1D3 Sanity (preset 5).
- Ten o’clock: the horses scream and fight the picket line. If one breaks loose it bolts onto the heath and stops at the well. By midnight it is a grey shape that crumbles when touched: 1/1D4 Sanity for anyone who sees it (preset 6).
- Eleven o’clock: Silas leaves his tent. If nobody stops him, he walks to the well and sits on the stones, smiling, glowing faintly. If he is held back he fights, then weeps, then begs.
- Midnight: the well fills with light. The colour pours up out of it like liquid, climbing the dead trees and running along the ground. 1/1D8 Sanity (preset 7).
- One o’clock: if the colour has fed on Silas or a horse, it gathers itself and shoots into the sky in a single column of light. Anyone who watches it go loses 1D3/1D10 Sanity (preset 8). If it has not fed, it sinks back into the well before dawn.

### Sealing the well
The best ending is to collapse the well before one o’clock. Someone must reach the well inside the reach, set the charge (see Act 3), light the fuse and get clear in about two minutes. Use the colour’s rules: POW rolls within ten yards, hit point loss every round. A Luck roll avoids flying stones when it blows. When the well collapses, the light goes out under the rubble with a sound like a long sigh.

### Saving Silas
Silas is not past saving if he is kept away from the well tonight. A First Aid or Medicine roll keeps him calm; a Persuade roll talks him out of walking. Tied up and taken out of the valley, he lives: grey-skinned, quiet and never quite well again.

sections.title: Endings and rewards
sections.text:
- The well sealed before one o’clock: the colour is buried. Each investigator gains 1D6 Sanity. If Silas lived, add 1D3 more for anyone who helped him.
- The colour rose into the sky: the heath stops growing, for now. Each investigator gains 1D4 Sanity. If the Keeper likes, next spring a surveyor’s stake near the well greys overnight.
- The investigators fled: no reward. Silas is not seen again. The reservoir floods the valley in April, and Arkham drinks its water.

### Epilogue
The Water Commission thanks the investigators for completing the survey. In spring the valley is flooded. Old Ammi Pierce, who sold his land for a good price, moves to Arkham and never drinks from a tap again.

sections.title: People
sections.text:
### Harlan P. Weeks, Arkham Water Commission
Late forties, round spectacles, always holding a folder. Wants the survey finished and no fuss. Pays fairly and on time.

### Ammi Pierce, the last neighbour
Near eighty, thin, sharp, frightened. Talks slowly and wanders. Loved the Gardners and has carried their story alone for forty years. He will not set foot on the heath, but he will lend a lantern, a shotgun he hasn’t fired since 1890, and his Bible.

### Silas Coombs, chainman
Nineteen, from Bolton, eager and friendly. Already touched by the colour: grey fingertips, poor sleep, a pull toward the well he explains away. He wants to be a proper surveyor like Mr Lund.

### Ezra Lund, chief surveyor
Fifty-five, ill in the Arkham hospital. Kind, methodical and frightened by what is happening to his body. Optional in Act 1.

sections.title: Clues at a glance
sections.text:
- The heath grows each year, and has moved since last week (Lund’s stakes, Ammi).
- Something stayed behind in the well in 1883 (Ammi, if asked what became of it).
- Silas and Lund both drank the well water and both are greying (Lund, Silas’s hands, Handout 6).
- The colour drained the Gardner family, their animals and plants (Ammi, Handout 5, the bones in the well).
- Earth and stone seemed to dull it (Handout 4).
- There is blasting powder in camp, meant for filling the well (Handout 1, the camp stores).

handouts.title: Letter from the Water Commission
handouts.where: Given to the investigators in Arkham
handouts.text:
ARKHAM WATER COMMISSION
Town Hall, Arkham, Massachusetts

October 12th, 1925

To the members of the western survey party,

The Commission engages you to complete the survey of the Gardner valley, west of Arkham, in readiness for the new reservoir. Mr. Ezra Lund, chief surveyor, has returned to Arkham unwell, and the work must be finished before the first snow.

You will find the camp at Pierce’s Corner, kept by the chainman, Silas Coombs. Mr. Lund’s field notes and instruments are with the camp stores.

Before the valley is flooded, the old well on the Gardner property (the place the country people call the blasted heath) is to be filled and made safe. A box of blasting powder, with fuse and caps, is in the stores for that purpose and for clearing stumps.

The Commission will pay four dollars a day and expenses, on presentation of the completed survey.

Yours faithfully,
Harlan P. Weeks
Secretary to the Commission

handouts.title: Survey map of the Gardner valley
handouts.where: Given to the investigators in Arkham
handouts.text: A hand-drawn survey map of the valley west of Arkham. The Arkham road comes in from the east along a stream. The survey camp is marked at Pierce’s Corner, with Ammi Pierce’s house a little further along the old road. The Gardner farm and its well sit in the middle of a grey patch labelled “blasted heath (approx. 5 acres)”. A dashed line marks the edge of the new reservoir, which will cover the whole valley floor. Survey stations are numbered along the line, the last ones by the heath.

handouts.title: Arkham Advertiser, June 1882
handouts.where: Advertiser back issues, or Ammi Pierce’s Bible
handouts.text:
THE ARKHAM ADVERTISER
Friday, June 23, 1882

STONE FROM THE SKY FALLS ON GARDNER FARM
Professors Examine Curious Visitor

A great stone fell from the heavens on Tuesday night upon the farm of Mr. Nahum Gardner, west of the town, landing beside his well with a noise heard as far as Pierce’s Corner. Mr. Gardner reports that it glowed in the darkness and that the grass about it was scorched.

On Wednesday three gentlemen of the Miskatonic University drove out to see it. They report that the stone was warm to the touch long after its fall, that it was soft enough to take the mark of a knife, and that it seemed to grow smaller as they watched. A piece was carried back to the college for study.

The professors confess themselves puzzled by its composition, and by a colour in it which, Mr. Gardner insists, he has never seen in anything before. The visitor has drawn a good many curious neighbours, and Mr. Gardner says they are welcome, so long as they keep off his corn.

handouts.title: Miskatonic laboratory notes, 1882
handouts.text:
Miskatonic University, Dept. of Chemistry. Specimen G-1 (Gardner fall). June 1882.

June 21. Specimen brought in a pail. Remains warm; does not cool in the cold room. Soft, malleable, takes a knife mark. Loses weight steadily: lighter each hour.

June 22. Spectroscope shows shining bands in positions none of us can match with any known element. Not affected by water, hydrochloric acid, nitric acid, aqua regia, ammonia, alcohol or ether. Magnetic: slightly.

June 23. Struck with a hammer, the specimen revealed a coloured globule within, glossy and brittle. On a second blow the globule burst. Nothing was left.

June 24. The specimen in the glass beaker is gone in the night. The beaker is gone with it. Burnt mark on the shelf.

N.B. (Prof. W.) The piece kept packed in clay for carriage seemed duller and cooler than the piece left in the open air. Earth and stone appear to damp it. Worth testing if more can be got.

June 28. Mr. Gardner reports the stone in his yard struck by lightning six times in Sunday’s storm and quite gone.

handouts.title: Nahum Gardner’s almanac
handouts.where: Under the kitchen floor of the Gardner house
handouts.text:
Pages from an 1883 farmer’s almanac, written in the margins in pencil and ink.

Oct 1882. Apples and pears biggest I ever grew. Bitter as gall. Not one fit to eat.

Jan 1883. Tracks in the snow by the barn. Woodchuck I think but wrong shape. Rabbits jumping too far.

March. Skunk cabbage come up colours I never seen. Thad says the plants shine at night. Told him not to talk foolish.

April. The cows give grey milk. Nabby says something in the air is at her.

June. Shut Nabby upstairs for her own good. She screams about things you cant see.

Aug. Thad gone to the well for water and dont come back. Merwin says he seen him in the well, shining.

Sept. Merwin gone. Zenas gone. All the stock gone grey and fall to pieces.

Oct. It come from that stone. It is in the well. It sucks the life out. It wants you to stay and you stay. Ammi is a good friend. Tell Ammi.

(The last lines are written over each other and cannot be read.)

handouts.title: Silas Coombs’s field book
handouts.where: On the well stones at the Gardner place
handouts.text:
A surveyor’s pocket field book. Most pages are station readings. The last pages read:

Sat 3rd. Sta. 41 to 46 along the heath. Mr Lund says the grey ground has moved past last weeks stakes. Must be wrong reading.

Mon 5th. Hot. Drank from the old Gardner well. Sweetest water I ever had. Mr Lund had two cups.

Wed 7th. Tired. Fingers ache. Ink wont come off.

Fri 9th. Mr Lund gone to Arkham sick. I am to keep the camp.

Sat 10th. Couldnt sleep. The dead trees by the heath move when there is no wind. They shine at the top.

Sun 11th. Not ink. Grey all down my hands now.

Mon 12th. I went to the well again. I didnt mean to. It is nice there. It is waiting for me to come down.

investigators.name: Margaret Halloran
investigators.blurb: Second-in-command of the survey now that Lund is ill. Knows explosives.

story.Personal description: Tall, weathered, practical clothes, a pencil behind one ear.
story.Ideology and beliefs: Everything has a cause you can measure.
story.Significant people: Ezra Lund, who gave her a job when no other firm would hire a woman engineer.

investigators.notes: Why you’re here: the Commission has made you acting chief of the survey. Lund is your mentor and you are worried about him.
investigators.gear: Theodolite and tripod, steel survey chain, field notebook, flashlight, pocket compass, blasting caps (in a tin).

investigators.name: Dr Samuel Ashcombe
investigators.blurb: County medical examiner, sent to check the camp after Lund’s illness.

story.Personal description: Grey moustache, good overcoat, reading glasses on a chain.
story.Ideology and beliefs: Do no harm, and do not panic the patient.
story.Significant people: His late wife, Clara, who died of a fever he could not name.
story.Treasured possessions: His medical bag, a gift from Clara.
story.Traits: Kind, careful, privately terrified of diseases he can’t diagnose.

investigators.notes: Why you’re here: Lund is your patient. You have never seen an illness like his, and you want to see where he caught it.
investigators.gear: Medical bag (bandages, morphine, sedatives, thermometer, scalpel), flask of brandy, flashlight.

investigators.name: Professor Ruth Kimball
investigators.blurb: Miskatonic geologist, surveying the bedrock for the dam.

story.Personal description: Small, quick, boots covered in mud, notebook always open.
story.Ideology and beliefs: The earth keeps records better than people do.
story.Significant people: Her old teacher, Professor Ward, who studied the 1882 meteorite and never spoke of it.
story.Treasured possessions: A rock hammer with her initials burned into the handle.
story.Traits: Curious to a fault, forgets to eat, argues with everyone.

investigators.notes: Why you’re here: the Commission wants a geologist’s report on the valley floor. You also want to see where the famous 1882 stone fell.
investigators.gear: Rock hammer, hand lens, sample bags, acid bottle, field notebook, lantern.

investigators.name: Tommy Briggs
investigators.blurb: Arkham Advertiser reporter writing a piece on the drowned valley.

story.Personal description: Cheap suit, loud tie, camera round his neck, grin always ready.
story.Ideology and beliefs: Every town has a story nobody wants printed.
story.Significant people: His editor, Mr Hatch, who thinks this is a two-paragraph job.
story.Treasured possessions: A Graflex camera bought on credit.
story.Traits: Charming, nosy, braver with a camera in his hands.

investigators.notes: Why you’re here: you sold your editor on a feature about the farms being drowned. You have heard there’s a ghost story in it.
investigators.gear: Graflex camera, a dozen plates, flash powder, notebook, pencils, cigarettes.

investigators.name: Walter Pruitt
investigators.blurb: The survey’s rodman, back from Arkham with supplies. Served in France.

story.Personal description: Broad, quiet, a scar through one eyebrow, army boots.
story.Ideology and beliefs: Look after the man next to you.
story.Significant people: Silas Coombs, the chainman, who reminds him of his kid brother.
story.Treasured possessions: A trench lighter from the Argonne.
story.Traits: Steady, slow to speak, doesn’t sleep well.

investigators.notes: Why you’re here: you’ve worked the survey all season. You left Silas alone at the camp and feel bad about it.
investigators.gear: Survey rods, hand axe, rope, lantern, hunting rifle and 20 rounds, trench lighter.
